forecasts.label: Interest payable

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Stockport says risk of seeking exceptional government support is rising, but not planned for 2027/28
news_drafts.lead:
Stockport Council's chief finance officer (its section 151 officer, the person with a legal duty to warn if the council cannot balance its books) has told the Corporate, Resource Management & Governance Scrutiny Committee that the risk of the council needing exceptional financial support is increasing. That is government permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and it is a last resort. The council does not intend to seek it for 2027/28.

The papers say this follows a "disappointing" multi-year funding settlement, which they say "materially weakened" the council's financial position. They also describe the underlying funding for essential local services as insufficient. The Summer Review of the council's medium-term financial plan says its ability to absorb further pressures is "increasingly constrained". It adds that the pressures "cannot be managed indefinitely through local measures alone". The council says they cannot be met by local efficiency measures alone and need sustainable national funding and policy reform. The same papers put the likelihood of a Section 114 notice, a formal warning that the council cannot balance its budget, as low in the short term.

For context, the papers cite the Local Government Association, which represents councils. It reports that 36 councils were granted exceptional financial support to set balanced budgets in 2026/27. It also warns that councils in England face a £7bn funding gap within three years. It attributes this to rising demand and costs in homelessness, children's services, adult social care, home-to-school transport and new national requirements.
news_drafts.paper_title: Part B Cabinet Response: Responding to Our Medium Term Financial Plan

news_drafts.headline: Stockport papers cite £5.6bn government funding to cover 90% of council SEND deficits to 2025/26
news_drafts.lead:
A Labour Group amendment before Stockport's Council Meeting on 1 October 2026 calls on government to fund council deficits caused by demand-led services that councils are required by law to provide. It points to what government has already done on one of them: around £5.6bn "to cover 90% of council SEND deficits built up to 2025/26, and a commitment to fund SEND centrally from 2028".

SEND stands for special educational needs and disabilities. Support for it is paid from the high needs part of school funding, the money for children with those needs, and it is one of the council's major cost pressures. The £5.6bn is a national figure covering councils across England. The material does not give Stockport's own share of it, or the size of the council's SEND deficit.

Under the commitment cited in the amendment, government would pay for SEND centrally from 2028 onwards, rather than councils meeting the cost from their own budgets. The material does not record the outcome of the vote on the amendment.
news_drafts.paper_title: Calling on government to fund council deficits caused by statutory demand-led services (Labour Group amendment)

news_drafts.headline: Valuation control weakness from prior audit still unresolved; £11.29m dwellings error found and corrected
news_drafts.lead: Stockport's auditors have found that a control weakness they identified in the previous year's accounts has not been fully addressed. The council's process for reviewing property valuations—checking that internal valuers' reports match the fixed asset register—remains ineffective despite management commitments to improve it. During their 2025-26 audit, external auditors identified a formula error in the dwellings valuation spreadsheet that overstated asset values by £11.29m, a material misstatement that the council corrected before finalising its accounts. The auditors also found a £1.89m overstatement in the Stockport Exchange Holiday Inn valuation, which the council assessed as not material and did not adjust. Separately, internal audit capacity has been cut by 85 days following staffing changes, leaving a 65-day shortfall against revised work plans and forcing deferral of ten audits including high-priority reviews of contract management and anti-fraud work.

findings.committee: Corporate, Resource Management & Governance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Academy school conversions reducing council insurance service revenue as converted schools can no longer purchase cover due to lack of insurable interest
findings.detail: The number of maintained schools converting to academy status continues to grow. Academies cannot purchase insurance from the council due to lack of insurable interest, while maintained schools have an alternative option to participate in the Government-backed Risk Protection Arrangement Scheme. This structural change is eroding the council's insurance service customer base.
findings.matters: This represents a structural decline in the insurance service's revenue base. Unlike temporary cost pressures, academy conversions are a permanent loss of revenue that will continue as more schools convert, requiring the service to either reduce costs or accept declining financial contribution.
findings.figures: Number of schools converting not quantified
findings.quote: Maintained schools now have the option to participate in the Government backed Risk Protection Arrangement Scheme. In addition, the number of schools converting to academy status continues to grow, which means they can no longer purchase insurance cover from the Council due to a lack of insurable interest.

findings.committee: Corporate, Resource Management & Governance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: High-rise residential blocks facing insurance market appetite reduction and higher premiums due to construction type concerns linked to Grenfell disaster
findings.detail: The council's high-rise residential blocks are facing insurance market pressure at renewal. Insurers have reduced appetite to insure blocks due to construction type concerns related to the Grenfell disaster. One block is now placed via Lloyd's of London market, while Zurich Municipal has imposed higher premiums on blocks classified as non-standard construction. The council is working with Stockport Homes Group to manage financial risk exposure.
findings.matters: This affects the council's housing-related assets (likely through Stockport Homes Group) and creates direct cost pressures through higher premiums. It reflects ongoing market concerns about residential safety standards that could extend beyond current holdings.
findings.figures: None specified in paper on premium amounts
findings.quote: At the last renewal, our insurers also had less appetite to insure our high-rise residential blocks. This is the due to their construction type and still links back to the Grenfell disaster. One block is now insured via the Lloyds of London market and ZM have imposed higher premiums on the blocks which they term non-standard construction.

findings.committee: Corporate, Resource Management & Governance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Unoccupied and high-risk property portfolio facing insurance market restrictions and higher costs as insurers limit coverage or refuse cover entirely
findings.detail: The council's unoccupied and high-risk property portfolio continues to face insurance market pressures. Insurers have imposed stringent policy terms, limited reinstatement values, or refused coverage. The council has had to place these properties with specialist insurers in the insurance market, creating higher administrative burden and increased premiums, though with more comprehensive cover.
findings.matters: This indicates the council holds property assets that the insurance market views as high-risk. Higher insurance costs are a direct budget impact, and the market's restrictions suggest potential coverage gaps if the council's property condition does not improve.
findings.quote: Our unoccupied and high-risk property portfolio continues to be impacted. Our insurers have imposed stringent policy terms, limited reinstatement values or refused coverage entirely. This has resulted in us seeking alternative cover from the insurance market. Although this is administratively more challenging and creates higher premiums, the resulting cover has been more comprehensive as the property is placed with a specialist insurer.

findings.committee: Corporate, Resource Management & Governance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Motor fleet insurance premiums increased at November 2025 renewal due to claim costs, claim numbers, and market-wide cost drivers including vehicle repair complexity
findings.detail: The council experienced increased motor fleet insurance premiums at renewal. The increases were driven by higher claim costs and claim numbers, compounded by broader insurance market conditions including shortage of vehicle parts, increasing technical complexity of vehicle repairs, and costs associated with electric vehicle repairs.
findings.matters: This is an ongoing cost pressure on the council's services that use vehicles. Repeated annual increases in insurance premiums reduce financial headroom and are particularly concerning given the council is already drawing on reserves to support the MTFP.
findings.figures: None specified in paper on amount of increase
findings.quote: At the November 2025 renewal, we saw an increase in motor fleet premiums, this was due to an increase in claim costs and numbers. However, premiums were also impacted by general insurance market conditions. A shortage of vehicle parts, the increasing technical nature of vehicles plus the cost of electric vehicle repairs, has heavily influenced claim costs across the UK.

findings.committee: Corporate, Resource Management & Governance Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Council recovered £940K in savings across five liability claims that progressed to court in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council successfully managed litigation on five liability claims during the year, achieving significant cost recovery. Two claims were won at trial, one discontinued before court, and two were settled pre-trial on an economic basis. The total savings achieved across all five claims was £940K, demonstrating effective use of the in-house legal capability.
findings.matters: This shows the council's in-house legal and insurance team is effectively defending claims and recovering costs, partially offsetting the upward pressure on insurance costs from higher claim volumes.
findings.figures: 5 claims to court; 2 wins, 1 discontinued, 2 settled pre-trial; £940K total savings
findings.quote: From April 2025 to March 2026 the Council progressed five liability claims to a court hearing. Of the five claims, two were won at trial, one claim discontinued before the court date and two were settled pre-trial on an economic basis. The savings made on all five claims totalled £940K.

daily_post.headline: Mid-year amendment approved to Minimum Revenue Provision policy to implement IFRS 16 Leases standard, requiring MRP to reflect lease asset value over life of lease rather than just lease liability
daily_post.lead: Shows accounting policy refinement in response to mandatory standard change; material to understanding revenue charges for capital-financed leases; peer councils implementing IFRS 16 track policy treatment differences and their revenue impact.
